name: Felix Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Felix. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say gets your name on it. What's a normal day at work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the office for a plumbing and heating firm, twenty engineers and a couple of apprentices. I take the calls, book the boiler services and breakdowns into the diary, sort the van routes, chase parts from the merchant and do the invoices off the engineers' job sheets. I've got a big wall planner with magnets for every van. Ray, the owner, says I'm the only reason the firm doesn't fall apart.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Winter, when every boiler in the county breaks on the same Monday. And money. Ray pays fair for a small firm but it's less than the big companies, and my girlfriend Ana and I have about two weeks of money in the bank after rent. There aren't other office jobs like this round here, it's mostly shops and the care home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we all get back to work. At the merchant's counter it's all anyone talks about, and I'd be glad to hear the end of it. I don't really post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means nothing changes, which is mostly fine. I'm still on the same money, still renting, still two weeks from trouble if Ana's salon has a quiet month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep the wall planner, keep the diary, keep chasing invoices. I'd maybe ask Ray for a bit more per hour in spring, and Ana and I would try again to put something by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Normal. A bit tired, because normal is already tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ray's firm pays less than the big ones. Is the firm itself steady?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady enough. People always need their heating fixed. The worry is Ray's sixty-three and his son Darren wants to take over and modernise everything, and Darren talks about booking apps like they're the answer to life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anyone at the firm tried any of these AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Darren tried an app for booking last year. It double-booked two engineers into the same loft and sent nobody to an old lady with no hot water. My wall planner is ugly, but it has never sent nobody to an old lady with no hot water.

say: I'd say **good, back to work**, and be glad the chatter stopped.
I'd keep quiet online; I'm **not a poster**.
think: Nothing changes, which is fine, but I'm still **two weeks** from trouble.
The bigger worry is **Darren taking over** and pushing booking apps.
do: Keep the **wall planner** and paper diary running the vans.
Ask Ray for a little **more per hour** in spring.
Try again with Ana to **put something by**.
feel: **Normal** and a bit **tired**, because normal is already tight.
S0.quote: My wall planner is ugly, but it has never sent nobody to an old lady with no hot water.
fieldNote: He's proud of a **paper system** that works and wary of apps that don't.
The **succession** from Ray to his son is the real threat in his mind.

steps.text: Keep running the twenty vans from the magnetic wall planner
Ask Ray for a small hourly raise in spring
Put a little aside each month with Ana

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see if it actually works before we bin what does. At the firm I'd be the sensible one asking who fixes it when it goes wrong. With mates I'd say the robots aren't coming to fix your boiler any time soon, so I'm half fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half fine is the honest bit. The engineers are safe for years, but everything I do is booking, ordering and answering customers, which is that whole list on the card. If Darren gets his booking system and parts ordering on autopilot, he doesn't need a full-time me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep being useful, and I'd make sure Ray sees what goes wrong with any new system. I'd cut back: no more Friday takeaways, cancel the streaming we don't watch. If they cut me to part-time, I'd ask if I could ride along with an engineer and learn the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like waiting for a call I know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Darren would love this. What happens when he takes over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Darren would bring the booking app back, a better one this time. Customers would book themselves online, and the parts would order off the job notes. I'd end up as the bloke who answers when the app confuses someone, maybe three days a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're the best at the job. Doesn't that count for something?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It counts with Ray. It won't count with Darren's spreadsheet. Being the best at sticking magnets on a board isn't a skill anyone's hiring for.

say: I'd say **let's see it work** before we bin what does.
I'd tell mates robots won't fix **your boiler** soon, so I'm half fine.
think: My work is **booking and ordering**, the exact list on the card.
With Darren's system, the firm **doesn't need** a full-time me.
do: Log every **new system** failure so Ray sees it.
Cut **takeaways and streaming** to stretch the money.
Ask to **ride along** with an engineer if hours are cut.
feel: **Dread**, like waiting for a call he knows is coming.
S1.quote: Being the best at sticking magnets on a board isn't a skill anyone's hiring for.
fieldNote: He clocks that the **engineers are safe** while his desk work is not.
He resists the tech, but **quietly**, not in open opposition.
The idea of **learning the trade** appears as a fallback, not a plan.

steps.text: Note every booking app failure and show Ray
Ask to ride along with an engineer if hours drop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad and someone should slow it down. At the firm I'd say it to anyone, the engineers, Ray, the merchant. I don't think shouting changes much, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my office job's gone. Whatever Darren thinks of me, a computer that can do any thinking work for free beats a bloke on a low wage with a wall planner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ray straight out for an apprenticeship as a plumber, even on apprentice pay, because it's hands-on. I'd hate the drop in money. Ana and I would cut back to the bone, maybe move somewhere cheaper with her sister for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted. Like the ground's gone soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI arrives 2028, robots 2031. What does that three-year gap mean in a plumbing firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the engineers keep going three years longer than me. If I can get on the tools, I buy three years, and three years is three years. After that I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ana talk about that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. Whether we can live on her wage plus apprentice pay. And probably whether we should put off getting married, because a wedding's the last thing we can afford.

say: I'd say it's **mad** and someone should slow it down.
I'd tell anyone at the firm, though shouting **changes little**.
think: My **office job is gone**; any thinking work is free now.
A low-wage bloke with a **wall planner** can't compete.
do: Ask Ray for a **plumbing apprenticeship**, even on apprentice pay.
Cut spending **to the bone** with Ana.
Consider moving in with **Ana's sister** to save rent.
S2.quote: If I can get on the tools, I buy three years, and three years is three years.
fieldNote: He uses the **robot gap** directly: hands-on work buys him time.
Resistant to tech, he's still willing to **take a pay cut** to switch.
Wedding plans become a **casualty** of the money squeeze.

steps.text: Ask Ray for a plumbing apprenticeship at apprentice pay
Cut household spending to rent, food and bills
Put the wedding off until money settles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years to sort ourselves out, so let's not waste them. At work I'd be more measured, talking to Ray about a plan. Same with mates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the office job goes, just slower. But five years means I could actually finish an apprenticeship before it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the apprenticeship within a year, while I've still got office hours to fall back on. Maybe split the week: two days in the office, three on the vans. I'd try to save a bit on the office days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less panicky. Like a long queue rather than a fire alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Would you still go for the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. A four-year apprenticeship done by 2030, and then I'm a qualified plumber with four years before the robots come. That's a proper plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version where you stay in the office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a bit, keeping the software running for Darren. But I'd be the last admin, not the first. I'd rather have a trade.

say: I'd say we have **a few years**, so let's not waste them.
I'd talk to Ray about **a plan**, calmly.
think: The office job **still goes**, just slower than in the fast picture.
Five years is enough to **finish an apprenticeship** before it does.
do: Start a **plumbing apprenticeship** within a year.
Split the week, **two days office**, three on vans.
Save a bit from the **office days**.
feel: **Worried**, but less panicky, like a long queue.
S3.quote: A four-year apprenticeship done by 2030, and then I'm a qualified plumber with four years before the robots come. That's a proper plan.
fieldNote: The extra time lets him **finish a trade** before thinking AI arrives.
He'd rather have **a trade** than be the last admin.
Still thin money, but **some control** returns.

steps.text: Start a four-year plumbing apprenticeship with Ray's firm
Work two office days a week and save that pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off and there's time to get ready. At work I'd probably not talk about it much. Ten years is a long time in a plumbing firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that I'll be fine with ten years if I don't just sit still, and the trouble is, sitting still is what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the office a couple of years, then start the apprenticeship once Ray's retirement is clearer. I'd keep saving what I can. I wouldn't touch AI unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Does that change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not right away, no. With ten years I'd wait and see what Darren does. If he's bringing apps in anyway, I'd move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the tools, hopefully, maybe running a van of my own. Ana always says I'm wasted on a desk.

say: I'd say it's **a long way off**, with time to get ready.
I wouldn't talk much at work; ten years is **a long time** in plumbing.
think: I'll be fine if I **don't sit still**.
Sitting still is **what I'm good at**, which worries me.
do: Stay in the office **a couple of years** and watch Darren.
Start the **apprenticeship** once Ray's retirement is clear.
Keep **saving** what he can and avoid AI tools.
feel: **Uneasy**, but able to live with it.
S4.quote: I'll be fine with ten years if I don't just sit still, and the trouble is, sitting still is what I'm good at.
fieldNote: He knows his own **inertia** is the risk.
His plan is a **delayed apprenticeship**, triggered by Darren's moves.
Thin savings and an exposed desk job keep the **income risk** real.

steps.text: Watch whether Darren brings booking apps in before acting
Start a plumbing apprenticeship once Ray retires
Save a fixed bit each month with Ana

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There's no time to learn a trade in two years. What would help is a decent apprenticeship wage for older starters, so a twenty-seven-year-old with rent can actually afford to switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who'll answer the phone at seven in the morning when someone's got no heating. The customers in this town are mostly old. Old customers with no heating at seven in the morning want a person, not an app.

headlineQuote: Old customers with no heating at seven in the morning want a person, not an app.
portrait: Felix runs the office of a **plumbing firm** with a magnetic wall planner and no AI.
He's on **low pay** with two weeks of savings and few local office jobs.
He sees the **engineers are safe** longer than him, and eyes an apprenticeship.
With more time he plans a **trade**; with two years he feels gutted and stuck.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to learn a trade.
whatWouldHelp: A decent **apprenticeship wage** for older starters with rent to pay.
